title: Trump Claims Direct Talks With Iran as War 'Hopefully' Nears End; UN Panel Flags US War Crimes in Iran
subhead: President Trump says he has spoken to Tehran 'directly' and that Iran 'wants to make a deal,' teeing up a UN General Assembly push with Gulf leaders next week. Separately, a UN fact-finding mission found 'reasonable grounds' the US committed war crimes in two Iran strikes, even as oil slid to a one-week low on Saudi reroutes.

sections.heading: Trump Claims Direct Talks With Iran Ahead of UN General Assembly Push
sections.body:
President Donald Trump told reporters Wednesday he has spoken to Tehran 'directly' and that the Iranians 'want to make a deal,' declaring the war, which began on Feb. 28, is 'hopefully' nearing its end, Fox News reports. Trump said he is weighing a 'big decision' between escalating military action to 'annihilate' the regime or pursuing a path to end the conflict.

The diplomatic maneuvering is converging on next week's UN General Assembly in New York. Trump is reported to be set to hold Iran talks with Gulf leaders in New York — Türkiye Today reports a New York meeting on postwar strategy — and the US has approved visas for Iran's President and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to attend the UN high-level meeting even with the sides at war, per The Hindu. House Speaker Mike Johnson went further, declaring the threat of an Iranian nuclear weapon has been 'taken care of' and that Republicans should pivot to lowering gas prices ahead of the midterms.

Iran has not confirmed the direct talks, and regional experts caution the regime is under 'extreme pressure' that could push it toward escalation or internal collapse, per the Middle East Institute's Nazee Moini.
sections.whyItMatters: A real or perceived channel to Tehran — however fragile — repositions the US-Iran conflict a week before UNGA, where a face-to-face or leader-level contact could test whether the 'wants to make a deal' line holds beyond rhetoric. It also gives Trump a domestic off-ramp ahead of midterms focused on gas prices.

sections.heading: UN Panel Finds 'Reasonable Grounds' of US War Crimes in Iran
sections.body:
A UN fact-finding mission said Thursday it found 'reasonable grounds' to believe US forces committed war crimes in two airstrikes in Iran, and that Iran committed crimes against humanity, AP and Bloomberg report. The mission's sharpest allegation, carried by Crypto Briefing, is a strike on a primary school in Minab that it says killed over 150 people including 120 children.

The findings land as Washington simultaneously pushes a diplomatic opening — a juxtaposition that puts political pressure on the 'deal' narrative at UNGA. The US State Department and the Trump administration have not publicly accepted the panel's conclusions, and the report carries no enforcement mechanism.
sections.whyItMatters: The war-crimes finding gives critics and neutral capitals documentation to attach to the US campaign right as Trump seeks a negotiated exit, complicating the messaging of a deal and feeding domestic and international pressure over the conduct of the conflict.

sections.heading: Oil Slides to One-Week Low as Saudi Arabia Reroutes Exports Through Oman
sections.body:
Oil prices fell to a one-week low Thursday, with Brent settling at $104.82 (down 1%) and WTI at $101.91, after reports that Saudi Arabia was moving crude through Oman to offset its damaged east-west pipeline, Reuters and Fox News report. State-run TASS noted Brent dipped below $102 intraday for the first time since Sept. 10. The drop came even with prices still holding above $100.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC that Saudi Arabia took 'quick action' to boost exports through the Strait of Hormuz with help from the US military. Damage to the Saudi east-west pipeline is worse than first assessed — three pumping stations confirmed damaged, with repairs potentially taking five to six weeks although partial flows could resume sooner, per reports circulating this week.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi rerouting via Oman partly cushions the pipeline outage, but it also signals the kingdom is pushing more barrels through Hormuz — the very chokepoint Iran claims to control — tying Saudi supply security more tightly to US naval protection and to the fate of the diplomacy.

sections.heading: US Approves $24.3 Billion F-35 Sale to Saudi Arabia
sections.body:
The US State Department approved the sale of 48 F-35 stealth fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a deal worth $24.3 billion, announced Thursday, Reuters and the Financial Times report. The approval comes as the kingdom is drawn deeper into the regional conflict — fighting Iran-backed drone and Houthi attacks on its oil infrastructure.

The sale follows years of Saudi lobbying and gives Riyadh the most advanced US fighter jet, a step that analysts have long flagged as controversial given recent Saudi strikes on Houthi targets and its role in the wider war. It signals Washington's continued arming of the kingdom even as it pursues a settlement with Tehran.
sections.whyItMatters: Approving the F-35 to Riyadh — during an active war with Iran — signals the US sees Saudi Arabia as its enduring regional security anchor regardless of how the Iran talks resolve, and gives Riyadh leverage it can use against Houthi and Iranian pressure on its energy infrastructure.

sections.heading: ExxonMobil Nears Orinoco Return as the US Rush Into Venezuela Deepens
sections.body:
US supermajor ExxonMobil is nearing a preliminary deal to invest in Venezuela's oil fields, with talks focused on the Petromonagas project in the Orinoco Belt, Mother Jones and World Energy News report. Exxon officials reportedly met Venezuelan counterparts this week. Energy Secretary Chris Wright called the broader push 'a milestone deal in making the Western Hemisphere the center of the global energy system.'

This follows this week's announcement that Continental Resources' Harold Hamm — a Trump ally — signed an MOU with PDVSA to develop and operate the 126,000-acre Ayacucho 2 block holding an estimated 30 billion barrels, and reports that Hamm's interests took over an extra-heavy crude field previously operated by a Chinese company, per Venezuelanalysis. Chevron earlier expanded in Venezuela with a $7 billion investment after the Trump administration seized President Nicolás Maduro in January.
sections.whyItMatters: The rapid succession of deals — Chevron, then Continental/Hamm, now ExxonMobil — shows Washington's Venezuela pivot is consolidating quickly, pulling US majors into the world's largest reserves, and squeezing Chinese operators out of Orinoco assets as Caracas trades access for revenue under US military threat.

sections.heading: LNG Price Surge Prices Out Asian Buyers, While Europe Faces a Lean Winter
sections.body:
Asia is set for its weakest September LNG imports in eight years as high spot prices deter buyers in China and South Asia, while Europe keeps paying up, Reuters reports across two analyses. Spot gas is fetching around $26 per million BTU, sending Europe shopping even as JERA chairman Yukio Kani warns spot prices will keep rising into winter on low inventories and Middle East supply disruption.

The reason Europe has no choice: the continent is entering winter with gas storage only about 70% full — a record low, according to a Reuters Breakingviews commentary. Asian buyers, meanwhile, are being priced out at a time of high Middle East disruption.
sections.whyItMatters: The crunch is being exported to Asia even as Europe 'is saved' — a reminder that the LNG market's pain is borne by price-sensitive emerging buyers in China and South Asia, reshaping who can afford energy in a war-driven supply squeeze with no obvious relief in sight.

bottomLine: The day's through-line is a rare convergence of diplomacy and accountability pressure on Washington: Trump claims direct contact with Tehran and a deal is within reach ahead of UNGA, while a UN panel asserts the US committed war crimes in its strikes. In the market, oil's slide to a one-week low on Saudi reroutes via Oman and the $24.3bn F-35 approval for Riyadh show Washington cementing its Gulf energy-security architecture regardless of the talks' outcome, even as ExxonMobil moves toward Venezuela's Orinoco and the LNG crunch pushes prices onto Asia's shoulders. The question now is whether the 'deal' rhetoric translates into anything concrete in New York next week — or remains positioning ahead of the midterms.
sources: Fox News, Reuters, TASS, Bloomberg, AP, The Hindu, Türkiye Today, Financial Times, Mother Jones, World Energy News, Venezuelanalysis, Crypto Briefing, Mercusys/WAM, Rigzone, Middle East Institute
